paper_metadata.title: Unsupervised quantum machine learning for fraud detection

summary: The paper evaluates quantum kernel methods using IQP feature maps for credit‑card fraud detection on a 500‑sample Kaggle dataset. Statevector simulations up to 20 qubits show that quantum kernels achieve about a 15% higher average precision than classical RBF kernels in unsupervised anomaly detection. All experiments are noiseless simulations and retain the same O(N_s^2) kernel Gram matrix scaling as classical methods.

experiments.description: Supervised fraud classification using a quantum kernel (IQP feature map with data re-uploading) on a credit card fraud dataset, compared against classical logistic regression and RBF SVC baselines.

algorithm.variant: quantum kernel SVM with IQP feature map and data re-uploading (d=3)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One feature per qubit; each feature is scaled and embedded via x-dependent rotations in an IQP-style circuit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Kernel-based supervised classification maximizing average precision on fraud vs genuine transactions.

problem_instance.description: Credit card fraud detection on anonymized transaction data with PCA-reduced features.

dataset_specification.description: 28 anonymized features; paper subsamples to 500 total samples with 25 fraud cases; PCA used to reduce dimensionality to N features matching qubit count; features standardized before PCA and scaled by eta=0.1 for quantum embedding.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Feature-wise standard scaling; PCA dimensionality reduction; subsampling to 500 samples with 25 fraud cases; quantum features scaled by 0.1 to keep phases below 2π.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision reported as a function of number of features/qubits; simulations run with statevector methods; comparison against classical baselines.

implementation_details.classical_solver: scikit-learn SVC with RBF kernel; logistic regression baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Random search hyperparameter tuning applied only to supervised models (LogReg and SVC); OC‑SVM uses default γ and ν values without extensive tuning.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average precision computed from predictions; Gram matrices assembled from kernel evaluations.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical RBF SVC / OC-SVM kernel methods
speedup_claims.conditions: kernel evaluation and Gram matrix construction both scale as O(N_s^2); comparison is empirical on a small benchmark dataset
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper reports empirical performance separation in average precision, not a proven computational speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Kernel evaluation and Gram matrix construction scale as O(N_s^2) for training and O(N_d N_s) for inference; per-circuit evaluation depends on shots.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical kernel methods also require O(N_s^2) Gram matrix evaluations; no asymptotic quantum speedup established.
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Observed performance separation at around 10-20 features/qubits; no asymptotic crossover established.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Observed empirical performance separation at ~20 qubits/features but no algorithmic complexity crossover demonstrated.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Authors suggest 50–100 qubits with deeper kernels and fast sampling may be required for potential practical advantage.
limiting_factors: No asymptotic speedup proven over classical kernel methods
Training requires O(N_s^2) Gram matrix evaluations identical to classical kernels

experiments.description: Unsupervised fraud/anomaly detection using a quantum kernel in one-class SVM, compared against classical RBF OC-SVM.

algorithm.variant: one-class SVM with IQP quantum kernel and data re-uploading (d=3)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One feature per qubit; PCA-reduced features are embedded into an IQP-style quantum feature map.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Novelty/anomaly detection by separating nominal transactions from anomalous fraud cases using one-class SVM with a quantum kernel.

problem_instance.description: Unsupervised credit card fraud detection on a public benchmark dataset using only nominal data for training OC-SVM.

dataset_specification.description: 28 anonymized features; paper subsamples to 500 total samples with 25 fraud cases; PCA used to reduce dimensionality to N features matching qubit count; nominal data used to train OC-SVM.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Feature-wise standard scaling; PCA dimensionality reduction; subsampling to 500 samples with 25 fraud cases; quantum features scaled by 0.1 to keep phases below 2π.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average precision reported versus number of features/qubits; unsupervised model trained on nominal data only; compared to classical OC-SVM with RBF kernel.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Standard scaling and PCA; hyperparameter tuning by random search and cross-validation AP.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average precision computed from predictions; Gram matrices assembled from kernel evaluations.

speedup_claims.conditions: empirical comparison on a 500-sample credit card fraud benchmark; quantum kernel uses IQP feature map with d=3 re-uploading
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper claims an empirical advantage in average precision, not a runtime or complexity speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Kernel evaluation and Gram matrix construction scale as O(N_s^2) for training and O(N_d N_s) for inference; per-circuit evaluation depends on shots.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical kernel methods also require O(N_s^2) Gram matrix evaluations; no asymptotic quantum speedup established.
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Observed quantum-classical separation in average precision begins past about 10 features and reaches about 15% at 20 qubits; no asymptotic crossover established.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Empirical performance improvement appears after ~10 features and reaches ~15% AP improvement at 20 qubits.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Potentially requires >50–100 qubits with scalable kernel evaluation and reduced shot requirements.
